description:
We are CyberAstro, a four-person team: Nurlana Nurullayeva, Nikita Shvedov, Ayesha Aliyeva and Rəna Rüstəmli. We love space, health tech and software that works when nothing else does.

For the "Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions" challenge we built ORBITA (Onboard Remote Biometric & Integrated Telemetry Assistant).
summary:
ORBITA is an offline-first desktop app for crew health on a deep-space mission. On the way to Mars, a message to Earth can take up to ~20 minutes one way, so astronauts cannot rely on real-time consultation with a flight surgeon.

Every day the astronaut enters 10 vital signs and symptom tags in a short check-up. A deterministic rules engine (52 rules, each traced to NASA, PubMed and other sources) compares them with the astronaut’s own preflight and 7-day baselines. It returns a clear Green/Yellow/Red status and says who to contact: no action needed, the crew medical officer, or the flight surgeon on Earth.

A layered body map, trend charts and animated alerts show what changed and where. A local language model (IBM Granite via Ollama) explains the results in plain words but can never change a status. On Red, the app prepares a message for the flight surgeon that the astronaut reviews and sends over a simulated delayed link.

Everything runs on one device with no internet and uses synthetic data. It addresses crew autonomy: early detection, the right escalation, and honest explanations when help from Earth is minutes away.
details:
What it does
ORBITA turns a 2-minute daily check-up into a clear, explainable health picture for an astronaut in Mars transit (demo: Day 40 of a 180-day transit, fictional astronaut, synthetic data).

  1. Daily check-up: blood pressure, heart rate, blood glucose, body temperature (rest/exercise), sleep, mood, body mass, skin symptoms, radiation dose rate and accumulated dose, plus 42 symptom and event tags and free-text notes. Metric and imperial units are supported. Input validation rejects impossible values (“Looks like a measurement error”), detects a likely mmol/L glucose entry, and blocks saving until the value is corrected.
  2. Personal baselines: each value is compared with the astronaut’s own preflight average or 7-day rolling average, not only with general limits. A heart rate of 80 bpm is “normal” on Earth, but +18 bpm above this astronaut’s normal of 62 bpm matters.
  3. Deterministic rules engine: 52 rules for 10 daily indicators. They come from our team’s research table, which compiles NASA Human Research Program pages, NASA-STD-3001 and peer-reviewed papers. Every rule quotes the table and lists its sources, and the app shows them on screen. The engine sets the colour and the escalation path. “Repeated readings” rules wait for confirmation and show “measure again tomorrow” instead of a false alarm.
  4. Radiation: dose-rate and accumulated-dose checks with illustrative mission settings derived from NASA-STD-3001 (600 mSv career limit, blood-forming-organ limits) and MSL/RAD cruise measurements (≈ 1.8 mSv/day). A dose-budget meter shows “72 of 600 mSv” and projects the dose at Mars arrival.
  5. Visual explanation: an interactive 4-layer body map (skin, muscles, organs, skeleton) with status markers on the organs. Each indicator has a 7-day and whole-mission trend chart with the “your normal” line. Each alert gets a large animation (beating heart, radiation symbol). Status is never shown by colour alone: there is always a word and an icon.
  6. Onboard assistant: layer 1 matches 16 verified symptom combinations from our research table, with sources, with no AI involved. Layer 2 is IBM Granite 3.3 (8B) running locally through Ollama. It explains the results in plain language but cannot change status or urgency. Its answers are automatically checked for diagnoses or false reassurance. Self-harm phrases trigger a support card. If the model is offline, a deterministic briefing is shown.
  7. Earth link: an asynchronous chat with a simulated Houston flight surgeon (~20 min one-way delay, shown 60× faster). It has an attached telemetry snapshot, an auto-prepared draft on Red status, and an automatic receipt.
  8. Crew access gate: NFC-badge + PIN demo profiles with separate local histories.

Benefits and intended impact

  • Earlier detection of trends that personal baselines reveal before general limits do.
  • Consistent, auditable decisions: the same input always gives the same result, with sources.
  • Less load on the crew: only 10 indicators every day, while 6 more (SpO₂, bone health, nutrition, exercise, vision, pulmonary function) serve as a knowledge base for the assistant.
  • The flight surgeon receives a structured, prioritised summary instead of a free-form message.

The same approach can help on Earth wherever a doctor is far away: Antarctic stations, ships, remote clinics.

Tools and technologies
TypeScript, React 19, Vite, Tauri v2 (Rust) for the desktop app; Recharts; Motion; lucide-react icons; Vitest (182 automated tests); Ollama with IBM Granite 3.3 8B. Fonts (Inter, Space Grotesk, JetBrains Mono, OFL) are bundled for fully offline use. No cloud services.

Creativity

  • We separate “deciding” from “explaining”: transparent rules decide, AI only explains, and the app checks the AI.
  • Personal baselines instead of one-size-fits-all limits.
  • The communication delay is a visible part of the design.
  • A calm, mission-control-style interface designed to be read in seconds.

Factors we considered

  • Safety: AI cannot override status; it gives no diagnoses; escalation is explicit.
  • Honesty: every rule shows its source; uncertain combinations are labelled “unverified”; all data is labelled SYNTHETIC; radiation thresholds are labelled illustrative.
  • Offline reliability and privacy: no network, data stays on the device.
  • Accessibility: large text, status words as well as colours, reduced-motion support.
  • Workload: a short daily check-up.
